description: Building a public sky-change explorer for Planet X & SPHEREx: enter any sky patch, watch a time-lapse, and get auto-flagged moving candidates (comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs) with measured accuracy. I’m a high schooler and Texas 4-H STEM Ambassador (astrophysics, AI/ML), leading science and pitching. Looking for: web/front-end devs, Python/astropy or image-processing folks, and a UI designer. Clear plan, defined roles, polished demo. Motivated beats expert, so join us!
summary:
When Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930, he only had two photos, a blink comparator, and a dot that moved. Today, NASA's SPHEREx mission takes photos of over a billion infrared objects across the entire night sky. Somewhere in that massive sea of light could be a new Dwarf Star, an elusive PlanetX, or even an undiscovered neighbor that no one knows about.

However, no scientist or astronomer can really find them all alone. Draconid Drift uses Tombaugh's time-tested discovery method for the modern world.

By combining modern SPHEREx infrared visits with archived 2MASS(2000) and WISE(2010) surveys, our platform creates a flipbook where the moving stars jumps out. Instead of forcing users into command lines with high latency times, our AWS pipeline helps serve multi-epoch sky videos, live pixel Diff subtraction, and even 102-band spectra in under 3 seconds. Users can even explore a 3D WebGl time machine where you can watch nearby stars march throughout their own planetary walk across thousands of years of real drift and simulated ones. Tested on NASA's own benchmark data, from the frozen brown dwarf WISE 0855 to Barnard's Star, Draconid Drift helps transform astrophysics into a platform that scientists can use to discover humanity's next world.
details: Draconid Drift is a temporal discovery engine that unlocks NASA's SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey. It transforms astronomical data into a visual experience where moving objects can reveal themselves. The core engine pairs with archival baselines from NASA's 2MASS and WISE missions. Users can play different frames like a movie through time, with frame-by-frame precision. We also added on-the-fly image processing where users can toggle between normal view and different modes to track stationary stars and isolate shifted objects. Incorporating ESA Gaia DR3 astrometry, we lifted 2D photos into an interactive 3D WebGL map where users can rotate around star fields and explore stars drifting across time. Supports include Right Ascension inputs along with Declination ones and access to all 5 of the project benchmarks. The backend consists of Python and a FastAPI, connecting to a cloud-native S3 storage bucket. This reduces latency times and allows native API processing. For scientific computing we used NumPy and AstroPy to handle spatial indexing. For 3D visualization, we used Three.js for the 3D space simulator and Aladin Lite for celestial globe navigation. The main factors we considered were reducing latency times, which we solved using cloud caching, and visual ergonomics, making our project look good. We want to transform raw data cubes into a gamified hunt where scientists can explore visual data from SPHEREx.
